A short story

The Ideal Boy

An evening by the pond with a grandfather and his grandson — and an old poem, understood anew.

Ten-year-old Neel sat idly at the edge of the pond, dipping his feet in the water, splash after splash. A cloud sat on his face. He'd come home that afternoon crying, after scraping himself a little while playing with friends. Whether it was games or schoolwork, backing away the moment something got hard had always been Neel's old habit.

His grandfather, Ratan Babu, came tapping his walking stick and sat beside him. He had been watching his grandson quietly for some time.

Neel“Grandpa, I'm never going to play football again. One little fall and my knee gets scraped — it hurts so much!”

Ratan Babu smiled gently and drew a small scrap of paper from his pocket.

Grandpa“Neel, shall I recite you a verse?”

Then, slowly, he began —

The Verse

Who wants that boy, tell me, who at every little word
brings tears to his eyes, whose head starts to swim?

Hands and feet — everyone has them — why this needless fear?
Can one who still has sense within just lie there, fallen?

Poem credit — Adarsha Chele ("The Ideal Boy") by Kusumkumari Das

Neel“That's the poem 'The Ideal Boy'! We read it at school.”

Grandpa“You read it, alright — but did you understand it?”

Neel stayed quiet.

Grandparan a hand over his hair and said, “Look, Neel — small hurts, fears, obstacles, they'll always come in life. Sometimes you'll fall, sometimes you'll make mistakes, sometimes you might even fail. But does that mean you give everything up out of fear?”

Neel slowly lifted his head.

Grandpa“Even brave people get hurt. Even they feel afraid. But they don't let that fear be the end of their road. They fall, and they get back up. They make mistakes, and they try again. That's really what it comes down to — not giving up.”

The words settled somewhere deep in Neel. He looked down at his dusty, scraped knee.

Neel“Grandpa, do I really give up that easily, over every little thing?”

Grandpasmiled sweetly. “Sometimes you do. But if you want to, you can change. You have hands, feet, a mind of your own. Most of all — you have the strength to try.”

Neel sat quietly for a while. Then, slowly, he stood up. His knee still hurt. But the fear inside him had eased, quite a bit.

Neelbrushed the dust from his knee and said, in a firm voice, “Grandpa, tomorrow evening I'm going back to the field.”

Grandpa“And if you fall again?”

Neelthought for a moment. “Then I'll get up again.”

Grandpa“And if it really hurts?”

Neel laughed this time.

Neel“Then maybe I'll cry too! But I won't run from the field.”

Grandparested a hand on his grandson's shoulder, a proud smile breaking across his face. “That's it. Today you didn't just read the poem — you understood what it means.”

That day, Neel didn't win any grand prize. He didn't pass any difficult exam.

But for the first time, he learned to stand up against his own biggest fear. And that was the day his journey toward becoming an ideal boy began.

Today's Lesson

It's alright to cry when it hurts. It's natural to feel afraid.

Real courage is getting back up again, and trying once more.

You can do it too. 🌱

Poem credit Adarsha Chele ("The Ideal Boy") — Kusumkumari Das
